title: III. The Brothers Make Friends
paragraphs: Ivan wasn't actually in a separate room, but in a spot shut off by a screen, so that he was out of sight of the other people there. It was the first room from the entrance, with a buffet along the wall. Waiters kept darting back and forth. The only other customer in the room was an old retired military man drinking tea in a corner. But the usual bustle was going on in the other rooms of the tavern — shouts for the waiters, the sound of corks popping, the click of billiard balls, the drone of the organ. Alyosha knew that Ivan didn't usually come to this tavern and disliked taverns in general. So he must have come here, Alyosha thought, simply to meet Dmitri as arranged. And yet Dmitri wasn't there.
“Shall I order you fish, soup, something? You don't live on tea alone, I assume,” Ivan cried, clearly delighted to have gotten hold of Alyosha. He had finished his dinner and was drinking tea.
“Let me have some soup, and tea afterward — I'm hungry,” Alyosha said cheerfully.
“And cherry jam? They have it here. Do you remember how you loved cherry jam when you were little?”
“You remember that? Let me have jam too — I still like it.”
Ivan rang for the waiter and ordered soup, jam, and tea.

“I remember everything, Alyosha. I remember you up until you were eleven — I was nearly fifteen. There's such a difference between fifteen and eleven that brothers are never companions at those ages. I don't even know whether I was fond of you. When I went away to Moscow, for the first few years I didn't think of you at all. Then when you came to Moscow yourself, we only met once, somewhere, I think. And now I've been here more than three months, and so far we've barely said a word to each other. Tomorrow I'm leaving, and I was just sitting here thinking how I might see you to say goodbye, and just then you walked by.”
“Were you really that eager to see me, then?”

“Very. I want to get to know you once and for all, and I want you to know me. And then to say goodbye. I believe it's always best to get to know people just before you leave them. I've seen how you've been looking at me these last three months. There's been a constant look of expectation in your eyes, and I can't stand that. That's why I've kept away from you. But in the end I've come to respect you. The little man stands firm, I thought. I may be laughing, but I'm serious. You do stand firm, don't you? I like people who stand firm like that, whatever it is they stand for, even if they're just such little fellows as you are. Your expectant eyes stopped annoying me — I grew fond of them in the end, those expectant eyes. You seem to love me for some reason, Alyosha?”
“I do love you, Ivan. Dmitri says of you — Ivan is a tomb! I say: Ivan is a riddle. You're a riddle to me even now. But I understand something in you, and I didn't understand it until this morning.”
“What's that?” Ivan laughed.
“You won't be angry?” Alyosha laughed too.
“Well?”
“That you are just as young as any other young man of twenty-three — that you're just a young and fresh and nice boy, green, in fact! Now, have I insulted you horribly?”

“On the contrary, I'm struck by a coincidence,” Ivan cried, warmly and good-humoredly. “Would you believe that ever since that scene with her, I've thought of nothing but my own youthful greenness — and just as though you guessed it, you bring it up. Do you know I've been sitting here thinking: even if I didn't believe in life, if I lost faith in the woman I love, lost faith in the order of things, were in fact convinced that everything is a disorderly, damnable, and perhaps devil-ridden chaos, if I were struck by every horror of man's disillusionment — still I would want to live, and having once tasted the cup, I wouldn't turn away from it until I'd drained it! At thirty, though, I'm sure to set down the cup, even if I haven't emptied it, and turn away — where, I don't know. But until I'm thirty, I know that my youth will triumph over everything — every disillusionment, every disgust with life. I've asked myself many times whether there is any despair in the world that could overcome this frantic, and perhaps unseemly, thirst for life in me, and I've come to the conclusion that there isn't — at least not until I'm thirty, and then I'll lose it on my own, I suspect. Some driveling consumptive moralists — and poets especially — often call that thirst for life base. It's a Karamazov trait, this thirst for life regardless of everything; no doubt you have it too — but why is it base? The centripetal force on our planet is still fearfully strong, Alyosha. I have a longing for life, and I go on living in spite of logic. Though I may not believe in the order of the universe, still I love the sticky little leaves as they open in spring. I love the blue sky, I love certain people — people one sometimes loves, you know, without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, though perhaps I've long ceased to have any faith in them; still, out of old habit one's heart treasures them. Here, they've brought your soup — eat it, it'll do you good. It's first-rate soup; they know how to make it here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha; I'll set off from here. And yet I know I'm only going to a graveyard — but it's a most precious graveyard, that's what it is! Precious are the dead who lie there; every stone over them speaks of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, and their science, that I know I'll fall to the ground and kiss those stones and weep over them — even though in my heart I'm convinced that it's long been nothing but a graveyard. And I won't weep out of despair, but simply because I'll be happy in my tears — I'll steep my soul in that feeling. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky — that's what it is. It's not a matter of intellect or logic; it's loving with one's insides, with one's gut. One loves the first strength of one's youth. Do you understand any of my tirade, Alyosha?” Ivan suddenly laughed.

“I understand it only too well, Ivan. One longs to love with one's insides, with one's gut. You put that so well, and I'm awfully glad that you have such a longing for life,” Alyosha cried. “I think everyone should love life above everything else in the world.”
“Love life more than the meaning of it?”

“Absolutely — love it regardless of logic, as you say; it has to be regardless of logic, and only then will one understand its meaning. I've thought so for a long time. Half your work is done, Ivan — you love life; now you only have to try the second half, and you're saved.”
“You're trying to save me, but perhaps I'm not lost! And what do you mean by your second half?”
“Why, one has to raise up your dead, who perhaps haven't died after all. Come, let me have my tea. I'm so glad we're talking, Ivan.”
“I see you're feeling inspired. I'm awfully fond of such _professions de foi_ from such — novices. You're a steadfast person, Alexey. Is it true you mean to leave the monastery?”
“Yes, my elder is sending me out into the world.”

“Then we'll see each other in the world. We'll meet before I'm thirty, when I'll start turning away from the cup. Father doesn't want to turn away from his cup till he's seventy; he dreams of hanging on to eighty, in fact — so he says. He means it all too seriously, buffoon though he is. He stands on a firm rock too — he stands on his sensuality, though after thirty, indeed, there may be nothing else to stand on.... But to hang on to seventy is vile; better to stop at thirty — one could retain ‘a shadow of nobility’ by deceiving oneself. Have you seen Dmitri today?”
“No, but I saw Smerdyakov,” and Alyosha quickly but in detail described his encounter with Smerdyakov. Ivan began listening anxiously and questioned him.
“But he begged me not to tell Dmitri that he'd told me about him,” Alyosha added. Ivan frowned and thought it over.
“Are you frowning because of Smerdyakov?” Alyosha asked.
“Yes, because of him. Damn him — I really did want to see Dmitri, but now there's no need,” Ivan said reluctantly.
“But are you really going so soon, brother?”
“Yes.”
“What about Dmitri and father? How is it going to end?” Alyosha asked anxiously.

“You're always harping on that! What do I have to do with it? Am I my brother Dmitri's keeper?” Ivan snapped irritably, but then suddenly gave a bitter smile. “Cain's answer about his murdered brother, wasn't it? Perhaps that's what you're thinking at this moment? Well, damn it all, I can't stay here to be their keeper, can I? I've finished what I had to do, and I'm going. Do you think I'm jealous of Dmitri — that for the past three months I've been trying to steal his beautiful Katerina Ivanovna? Nonsense, I had business of my own. I finished it. I'm going. I finished it just now — you were a witness.”
“At Katerina Ivanovna's?”

“Yes, and I've set myself free once and for all. And after all, what do I have to do with Dmitri? Dmitri doesn't enter into it. I had my own business to settle with Katerina Ivanovna. You know, on the contrary, that Dmitri behaved as if there were some understanding between us. I never asked him to do it, but he solemnly handed her over to me and gave us his blessing. The whole thing is absurd. Ah, Alyosha, if you only knew how light my heart is now! Would you believe it, I was sitting here eating my dinner and was on the verge of ordering champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Tfoo! It's been going on nearly six months, and all at once I've thrown it off. Even yesterday I'd never have guessed how easy it would be to put an end to it if I wanted to.”
“You're talking about your love, Ivan?”

“About my love, if you like. I fell in love with the young lady, I tormented myself over her, and she tormented me. I sat brooding over her ... and all at once it collapsed! I spoke this morning with inspiration, but then I left and roared with laughter. Would you believe it? Yes, it's the literal truth.”
“You seem very cheerful about it now,” observed Alyosha, looking into his face, which had suddenly brightened.

“But how could I know that I didn't care for her in the slightest? Ha ha! It turns out that after all, I didn't. And yet how she drew me! How attractive she was just now when I made my speech! And do you know, she attracts me terribly even now — and yet how easy it is to leave her. Do you think I'm bragging?”
“No, only perhaps it wasn't love.”

“Alyosha,” Ivan laughed, “don't philosophize about love — it doesn't suit you. How you plunged into the discussion this morning! I forgot to kiss you for it.... But how she tormented me! It really was sitting at the side of a ‘laceration.’ Ah, she knew how I loved her! She loved me, not Dmitri,” Ivan insisted gaily. “Her feeling for Dmitri was simply a self-laceration. Everything I told her just now was perfectly true — but the worst of it is, it may take her fifteen or twenty years to realize that she doesn't care for Dmitri and loves me, whom she torments — and perhaps she'll never realize it at all, despite the lesson she got today. Well, it's better this way; I can simply go away for good. By the way, how is she now? What happened after I left?”
Alyosha told him she had become hysterical, and that he'd heard she was now unconscious and delirious.
“Isn't Madame Hohlakov exaggerating?”
“I don't think so.”
“I'll have to find out. Nobody dies of hysterics, though. It doesn't matter. God gave women hysterics as a relief. I won't go to her at all. Why push myself forward again?”
“But you told her that she'd never cared for you.”
“I did that on purpose. Alyosha, shall I call for champagne? Let's drink to my freedom. Ah, if you only knew how glad I am!”
“No, brother, we'd better not drink,” Alyosha said suddenly. “Besides, I feel somehow depressed.”
“Yes, you've been depressed for a long time; I've noticed.”
“So you've decided to leave in the morning, then?”

“Morning? I didn't say I was going in the morning.... But perhaps I will. Would you believe it, I only dined here today to avoid dining with the old man — I loathe him so much. As far as he's concerned, I'd have left long ago. But why are you so worried about my leaving? We've got plenty of time before I go — an eternity!”
“If you're leaving tomorrow, what do you mean by an eternity?”

“But what does that matter to us?” Ivan laughed. “We've got enough time for our talk, for what brought us here. Why do you look so surprised? Answer me: why have we met here? To talk of my love for Katerina Ivanovna, of the old man and Dmitri? Of foreign travel? Of the fatal position of Russia? Of the Emperor Napoleon? Is that it?”
“No.”

“Then you know what for. It's different for other people, but we — in our green youth — have to settle the eternal questions first of all. That's what we care about. Young Russia is talking about nothing but the eternal questions now. And just when the old folks are all taken up with practical questions. Why have you been looking at me expectantly for the last three months? To ask me, ‘What do you believe, or don't you believe at all?’ That's what your eyes have been meaning for these three months, isn't it?”
“Perhaps so,” Alyosha smiled. “You're not laughing at me now, are you, Ivan?”

“Me, laughing? I don't want to wound my little brother, who's been watching me with such expectation for three months. Alyosha, look me straight in the eye! Of course I'm just such a little boy as you are, only not a novice. And what have Russian boys been doing up to now — some of them, I mean? In this stinking tavern, for instance — right here — they meet and sit down in a corner. They've never met before in their lives, and when they leave the tavern, they won't meet again for forty years. And what do they talk about in that brief pause in the tavern? About the eternal questions — about the existence of God and immortality. And those who don't believe in God talk about socialism or anarchism, about transforming all humanity on a new pattern — so it all comes to the same thing; they're the same questions turned inside out. And masses, masses of the most original Russian boys do nothing but talk about the eternal questions! Isn't it so?”

“Yes, for true Russians the questions of God's existence and of immortality, or, as you say, the same questions turned inside out, come first and foremost, of course, and so they should,” Alyosha said, still watching his brother with the same gentle, inquiring smile.

“Well, Alyosha, it's sometimes very unwise to be Russian at all — but you can hardly imagine anything stupider than the way Russian boys spend their time. Yet there's one Russian boy named Alyosha whom I'm awfully fond of.”
“How nicely you slipped that in!” Alyosha laughed suddenly.
“Well, tell me where to begin — give the orders. The existence of God, eh?”
“Begin wherever you like. You declared yesterday at father's that there is no God.” Alyosha looked searchingly at his brother.

“I said that yesterday at dinner on purpose, to tease you, and I saw your eyes glow. But now I've no objection to discussing it with you, and I say that very seriously. I want to be friends with you, Alyosha, because I have no friends and want to try having one. Well, just imagine — perhaps I too accept God,” Ivan laughed; “that's a surprise to you, isn't it?”
“Yes, of course, if you're not joking now.”

“Joking? I was told at the elder's yesterday that I was joking. You know, dear boy, there was an old sinner in the eighteenth century who declared that if God didn't exist, He would have to be invented. _S'il n'existait pas Dieu, il faudrait l'inventer._ And man has indeed invented God. And what's strange — what would be marvelous — is not that God really exists; the marvel is that such an idea, the idea of the necessity of God, could enter the head of such a savage, vicious beast as man. So holy it is, so touching, so wise, and such a credit to man. As for me, I long ago resolved not to think about whether man created God or God man. And I won't go through all the axioms laid down by Russian boys on the subject, all derived from European hypotheses — because what's a hypothesis there is an axiom for the Russian boy, and not only for the boys but for their teachers too, since our Russian professors are often the very same boys themselves. So I skip all the hypotheses. What are we aiming at now? I'm trying to explain to you as quickly as possible my essential nature — that is, what kind of man I am, what I believe in, and what I hope for. That's it, isn't it? And so I tell you that I simply accept God. But mark this: if God exists and if He really did create the world, then, as we all know, He created it according to the geometry of Euclid and the human mind with the conception of only three dimensions in space. Yet there have been, and still are, geometers and philosophers, even some of the most distinguished, who doubt whether the whole universe — or, to put it more broadly, the whole of being — was created only in Euclid's geometry; they even dare to dream that two parallel lines, which according to Euclid can never meet on earth, may meet somewhere in infinity. I've come to the conclusion that since I can't understand even that, I can't expect to understand about God. I humbly acknowledge that I have no faculty for settling such questions; I have a Euclidian, earthly mind, and how could I solve problems that aren't of this world? And I advise you never to think about it either, my dear Alyosha — especially about God, whether He exists or not. All such questions are completely out of place for a mind created with an idea of only three dimensions. And so I accept God, and am glad to, and what's more, I accept His wisdom, His purpose — which are utterly beyond our understanding; I believe in the underlying order and in the meaning of life; I believe in the eternal harmony in which, they say, we'll one day be blended together. I believe in the Word to which the universe is striving, and which Itself was ‘with God,’ and which Itself is God, and so on, and so on, to infinity. There are all sorts of phrases for it. I seem to be on the right path, don't I? And yet would you believe it, in the final result I don't accept this world of God's, and although I know it exists, I don't accept it at all. It isn't that I don't accept God — you must understand — it's the world created by Him that I don't and can't accept. Let me make this clear. I believe like a child that suffering will be healed and made up for, that all the humiliating absurdity of human contradictions will vanish like a pitiful mirage, like the despicable fabrication of man's impotent and infinitely small Euclidian mind — that in the world's finale, at the moment of eternal harmony, something so precious will come to pass that it will suffice for all hearts, for the consolation of all resentments, for the atonement of all the crimes of humanity, of all the blood they've shed; that it will make it not only possible to forgive, but to justify, all that has happened with men — but even though all that may come to pass, I don't accept it. I won't accept it. Even if parallel lines do meet, and I see it myself, I'll see it and say they've met, but still I won't accept it. That's what's at the root of me, Alyosha; that's my creed. I'm serious about what I say. I began our talk as stupidly as I could on purpose, but I've led up to my confession, because that's all you want. You didn't want to hear about God, but only to know what the brother you love lives by. And so I've told you.”
Ivan concluded his long tirade with marked and unexpected feeling.
“And why did you begin ‘as stupidly as you could’?” Alyosha asked, looking dreamily at him.

“First of all, for the sake of being Russian. Russian conversations on such subjects are always carried on with inconceivable stupidity. And secondly, the stupider one is, the closer to reality. The stupider one is, the clearer one is. Stupidity is brief and artless, while cleverness wriggles and hides itself. Cleverness is a knave, but stupidity is honest and straightforward. I've brought the conversation around to my despair, and the more stupidly I've presented it, the better for me.”
“You'll explain why you don't accept the world?” Alyosha said.

“Of course I will — it's no secret; that's what I've been leading up to. Dear little brother, I don't want to corrupt you or to shake you from your stronghold; perhaps I want to be healed by you.” Ivan smiled suddenly, exactly like a little gentle child. Alyosha had never seen such a smile on his face before.
